metadata.summary: This international, survey-based expert consensus addresses immunomodulatory therapy for non-infectious uveitis during the COVID-19 pandemic. It considers treatment decisions according to suspected or confirmed COVID-19, exposure history and systemic risk, covering corticosteroids, conventional immunosuppressive drugs and biologics. It also addresses NSAIDs for scleritis, hydroxychloroquine and measures intended to reduce infection exposure; the authors note that the guidance rests on expert opinion amid limited evidence.

target_population: patients with NIU receiving or being considered for IMT
otherwise healthy patients with close contact with an individual with COVID-19

toxicities.event: Increased susceptibility to infections during IMT; the effect on COVID-19 infection and outcomes remains uncertain
recognition: Clinical features compatible with COVID-19, including upper respiratory tract infection, indicate suspected disease when testing has not been performed or is unavailable.
Compatible clinical features together with a positive SARSCoV-2 test identify confirmed disease.
prevention: Use hand hygiene, physical distancing and masks to reduce exposure.

toxicities.event: Adrenal insufficiency associated with abrupt cessation of oral corticosteroids
prevention: Taper oral corticosteroids rather than stopping them abruptly when discontinuation is indicated.
toxicities.dose_modifications: The experts recommended tapering instead of abrupt cessation; the document provides no tapering schedule.

prophylaxis.recommendation: Experts agreed on personal hand hygiene, avoiding crowds, wearing masks and self-isolation.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients with NIU receiving conventional IMT or biologics

prophylaxis.recommendation: Avoid hospital visits that are not useful and postpone long-term follow-up. When feasible, use electronic communication or telehealth to check for signs of infection and reduce non-urgent clinic visits.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients with NIU receiving conventional IMT or biologics; patients with uveitis attending follow-up

prophylaxis.recommendation: Routinely apply physical distancing, hand hygiene and mask use during follow-up to reduce infection risk.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients with uveitis presenting for follow-up

infection_management.pathogen_or_syndrome: SARS-CoV-2 exposure through close contact with a person with COVID-19
infection_management.prevention: Experts agreed on hand hygiene, avoiding crowds, masks, self-isolation and reducing unnecessary hospital visits for patients with NIU receiving conventional IMT or biologics.
infection_management.management: For otherwise healthy patients with a contact history, experts preferred local corticosteroids over starting systemic treatment in the specified risk groups. They advised against starting biologics in high-risk and very high-risk patients, and against starting conventional immunosuppressive drugs in very high-risk patients. Intravenous methylprednisolone should be avoided in high-risk and very high-risk patients with a contact history.

infection_management.prevention: Physical distancing, hand hygiene and masks were recommended to reduce exposure; electronic or telehealth contact was encouraged when feasible to monitor for signs of infection.
infection_management.management: Experts agreed not to initiate systemic corticosteroids, intravenous methylprednisolone, conventional immunosuppressive drugs or biologics for NIU in sick patients, regardless of risk group. They preferred local corticosteroids over starting or increasing systemic corticosteroids. Higher-dose oral corticosteroids should be tapered in all risk groups; experts also supported reducing or tapering low-dose oral corticosteroids in high-risk and very high-risk patients, but reached no consensus on maintaining, reducing or stopping low-dose oral corticosteroids in increased risk patients. Conventional immunosuppressive drugs and biologics should be reduced or stopped rather than maintained. The document states that the use of tocilizumab for NIU in a patient with COVID-19 is unknown.

conditions.name: non-infectious uveitis
conditions.description: A group of inflammatory eye diseases that can threaten vision and may coexist with systemic inflammatory disease. The guidance addresses immunomodulatory treatment during the COVID-19 pandemic.
conditions.clinical_presentation: The diseases within this group vary in clinical course, visual outcomes and treatment requirements.

subtypes.name: Behçet
subtypes.distinguishing_features: The authors identify this as an example of NIU in which rapid reduction of IMT may cause visual loss that could be permanent.

subtypes.name: Vogt–Koyanagi–Harada disease
subtypes.distinguishing_features: The authors identify this as an example of NIU in which rapid reduction of IMT may cause visual loss that could be permanent.

prognostic_tools.name: British Society of Rheumatology
components: Use of immunosuppressive drugs other than biologics
Active systemic inflammatory disease associated with NIU
Other comorbidities or multisystem disease involving the heart, lung and/or kidney

risk_groups.criteria: Patients with NIU receiving immunosuppressive drugs, excluding biologics.
Patients with NIU who have one of the listed risk factors.
Patients with NIU who have two or more of the listed risk factors.

prognostic_tools.interpretation: The guidance uses this stratification when considering systemic risk during the COVID-19 pandemic and describes it as a surrogate for uveitis severity.

follow_up.schedule: The experts supported postponing long-term follow-up and avoiding hospital visits that are not productive; no fixed follow-up interval is specified.
long_term_effects: Rapid reduction of IMT in some forms of NIU may lead to visual loss that could be permanent.
follow_up.survivorship_notes: When feasible, electronic or telehealth contact is encouraged to watch for signs of infection and reduce non-urgent clinic visits.

conditions.name: scleritis
conditions.description: An inflammatory eye condition addressed separately in the guidance's discussion of NSAIDs during the COVID-19 pandemic.

conditions.name: COVID-19
conditions.description: The infection status considered alongside systemic risk factors when making IMT decisions for patients with NIU.
conditions.epidemiology: The guidance states that everyone is susceptible to SARSCoV-2 infection, but that robust data were lacking on whether systemic inflammatory disease or IMT increases infection risk or worsens outcomes in people who develop COVID-19.
conditions.clinical_presentation: The survey describes suspected or confirmed illness as having clinical features compatible with COVID-19, which may include upper respiratory tract infection.

subtypes.distinguishing_features: Clinical features compatible with COVID-19 are present, but diagnostic testing has not been performed or is unavailable.

subtypes.name: sick patient with COVID-19
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Clinical features compatible with COVID-19 are present together with a positive test for SARSCoV-2 infection.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Distinguish confirmed infection from suspected COVID-19 in the survey scenarios.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A positive result, together with compatible clinical features, defines the survey's confirmed-infection group.

artifacts.title: Expert responses on IMT during COVID-19 in increased risk patients (n=139)
artifacts.source_heading: Consensus on increased risk patients with NIU

rows: To be preferred to systemic therapy
To be preferred to increasing the dose of systemic therapy

artifacts.description: Each result gives the number and percentage of the 139 experts supporting the stated action for that patient group. The table defines increased risk as uveitis or rheumatologic disease treated with immunosuppressives but not biologics. An action met the study’s consensus threshold only when more than 75% of experts supported it; other percentages must not be interpreted as consensus.
artifacts.summary: The table compares responses about corticosteroids and conventional IMT across four COVID-19 exposure or illness groups in increased risk patients.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: It identifies which treatment decisions had expert consensus and distinguishes them from options that were assessed but did not reach the consensus threshold.

artifacts.title: Expert responses on IMT during COVID-19 in high-risk patients (n=139)
artifacts.source_heading: Consensus on high-risk and very high-risk patients with NIU

rows: To be preferred to systemic therapy
To be preferred to increasing the dose of systemic therapy

artifacts.description: Entries report the number and percentage of the 139 experts supporting each action. The table defines high risk as uveitis or rheumatologic disease with one listed risk factor, including biologic use, high-dose or multiple immunosuppressives, active associated systemic disease, specified comorbidities, neutropenia, smoking, pregnancy, older age, or previous infection during IMT. Consensus required support from more than 75% of experts.
artifacts.summary: The table compares proposed actions for corticosteroids, conventional IMT, biologics and Tocilizumab in high-risk patients according to COVID-19 exposure or illness status.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: It separates actions supported by expert consensus from those without consensus, particularly when infection is suspected or confirmed.

artifacts.clinical_relevance: It shows where expert consensus supports maintaining, changing or avoiding treatment in patients with the greatest number of defined systemic risk factors.

special_populations.considerations: Patients with NIU receiving immunosuppressive drugs other than biologics.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: For otherwise healthy patients, oral corticosteroids may be started when needed for newly diagnosed NIU; low-dose oral corticosteroids are continued, including after COVID-19 contact. In active NIU, local corticosteroids are preferred over increasing systemic corticosteroids. After contact, local treatment is preferred over starting systemic corticosteroids in patients not taking oral corticosteroids. Otherwise healthy patients with active NIU may start or continue conventional immunosuppressive drugs. With suspected or confirmed COVID-19, do not start oral corticosteroids, intravenous methylprednisolone or conventional immunosuppressive drugs; reduce higher-dose oral corticosteroids to a safer lower dose, prefer local over new or increased systemic corticosteroids, and decrease or stop conventional immunosuppressive drugs. There was no consensus on whether to maintain, decrease or stop low-dose oral corticosteroids in these sick patients.

special_populations.considerations: Patients with NIU and one risk factor: biologics use; high doses or multiple immunosuppressive drugs; active associated systemic inflammatory disease; comorbidities or multisystem disease involving the heart, lung and/or kidney; neutropenia; smoking; pregnancy; age more than 60 years; or previous infection during IMT.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: In otherwise healthy patients, maintain low-dose oral corticosteroids and continue conventional immunosuppressive drugs and biologics without dose reduction. Prefer local corticosteroids over increasing systemic treatment, regardless of COVID-19 contact; after contact, also prefer local treatment over starting systemic corticosteroids in patients not taking oral corticosteroids, avoid intravenous methylprednisolone and do not start biologics. With suspected or confirmed COVID-19, do not start oral corticosteroids, conventional immunosuppressive drugs or biologics. Decrease and/or stop systemic corticosteroids, and decrease and/or stop conventional immunosuppressive drugs and biologics; prefer local corticosteroids over starting or increasing systemic treatment. Taper oral corticosteroids rather than stopping them abruptly because of adrenal insufficiency risk.

special_populations.considerations: Patients with NIU and two or more of the systemic risk factors used to define the high-risk category.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: In otherwise healthy patients, maintain low-dose oral corticosteroids and continue conventional immunosuppressive drugs and biologics. Prefer local corticosteroids over starting or increasing systemic corticosteroids, regardless of COVID-19 contact. After contact, avoid intravenous methylprednisolone and do not start conventional immunosuppressive drugs or biologics. With suspected or confirmed COVID-19, do not start oral corticosteroids, conventional immunosuppressive drugs or biologics. Decrease and/or stop systemic corticosteroids, and decrease and/or stop conventional immunosuppressive drugs and biologics; prefer local corticosteroids over starting or increasing systemic treatment. Taper oral corticosteroids rather than stopping them abruptly because of adrenal insufficiency risk.

special_populations.population: Patients with Behçet or Vogt–Koyanagi–Harada disease
special_populations.considerations: The document cautions that some NIU, including these diseases, may develop visual loss that could be permanent if IMT is reduced rapidly. Its consensus guidance may therefore not apply equally to every disease within NIU.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Assess the individual patient's circumstances and balance any IMT reduction against the risk of sight-threatening inflammation; the document gives no disease-specific dose adjustment.

document_sections.heading: ABSTRACT
document_sections.content: Background: Immunomodulatory therapy (IMT) is frequently considered for systemic treatment of non-infectious uveitis (NIU). Concern about infections during the coronavirus disease2019 (COVID-19) pandemic created an urgent need for guidance on its use. Methods: An international, cross-sectional survey asked uveitis specialists to assess scenarios developed by an expert steering committee. A total of 139 experts contributed to consensus statements concerning initiation, continuation, reduction and cessation of systemic and local corticosteroids, conventional immunosuppressive agents and biologics. The survey included 216 statements and 31 additional questions about general care, including non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and hydroxychloroquine. Results: The clearest consensus opposed initiating IMT in patients with suspected or confirmed COVID-19 and favored local over systemic corticosteroids in patients at high or very high risk of severe or fatal COVID-19. Experts agreed on initiating NSAIDs for scleritis in otherwise healthy patients, but did not reach consensus on starting hydroxychloroquine in any risk group. Conclusion: The proposed guidance draws on international expert opinion and clinical experience because medical evidence was lacking.

document_sections.heading: INTRODUCTION
document_sections.content: NIU encompasses inflammatory eye diseases that threaten vision and can accompany systemic inflammatory disorders. IMT is often considered for systemic management. Corticosteroids may be given topically, peribulbarly, intravitreally, orally or intravenously; conventional immunosuppressive agents and biologics are commonly used when prolonged treatment and a corticosteroid-sparing strategy are needed. Suppression of immune responses makes infection an important concern with IMT. The WHO declared COVID-19 a pandemic on 11 March 2020. Anyone can acquire severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARSCoV-2), while people receiving IMT might face additional infection risk, more severe COVID-19 or death. Guidance for patients with uveitis was therefore urgently needed. Literature on this question was virtually absent. Robust evidence had not established whether systemic inflammatory disease or IMT worsened infection risk or outcomes after COVID-19; reports involving rheumatic disease were few, and applying their findings to SARS-CoV-2 infection and ocular inflammation was problematic. The study sought to synthesize international uveitis specialists’ views on managing IMT during the pandemic. It was supported by the International Uveitis Study Group (IUSG), International Ocular Inflammation Society (IOIS), Uveitis Society of India (USI) and Foster Ocular Immunology Society (FOIS).

document_sections.heading: METHODS
document_sections.content: An expert steering committee helped formulate 216 statements about IMT for NIU during COVID-19, together with 31 questions on broader management of inflammatory eye disease. An interactive web survey distributed these items to members of IUSG, IOIS, USI and FOIS. The broader questions addressed NSAIDs for scleritis: non-selective COX inhibitors comprising acetates (diclofenac, indomethacin, sulindac), fenamates (mefenamic acid), oxicams (piroxicam), propionates (ibuprofen, ketoprofen, naproxen), pyrazolones (phenylbutazone), salicylates (aspirin, diflunisal) and flurbiprofen; selective COX2 inhibitors comprising meloxicam, nimesulide, celecoxib, etoricoxib and valdecoxib; and hydroxychloroquine. Agreement by more than 75% of experts defined consensus for an IMT statement; for a general question, consensus required more than 75% to give the same answer. Experts answered yes or no to scenarios defined by possible COVID-19 and systemic risk factors, including the number of IMT drugs. Four infection-status groups were specified: a person without infection signs or apparent contact with confirmed COVID-19; a person otherwise healthy after close contact with someone infected; a symptomatic person with suspected COVID-19, including possible upper respiratory tract infection, for whom diagnostic testing had not been performed or was unavailable; and a symptomatic person with a positive SARSCoV-2 test. The survey covered local and oral corticosteroids, intravenous methylprednisolone, conventional immunosuppressive drugs and biologics. Corticosteroids were kept separate from conventional IMT to distinguish responses. Separate tocilizumab questions addressed anecdotal observations and ongoing trials suggesting possible control of cytokine storm in COVID-19. Experts evaluated each combined scenario from their experience and opinions. In April 2020, 139 international experts completed the survey. Ethics approval covered a survey of expert opinions without patient data, and the study followed the Declaration of Helsinki.

document_sections.heading: RESULTS Description of participants
document_sections.content: The April 2020 survey included 139 uveitis specialists. Experience treating NIU exceeded 15 years for 42.4% (n=59/139), while 38.84% (n=54/139) treated more than 300 patients with IMT each year. Participants practiced in Asia (n=44/139, 31.7%), Europe (n=43/139, 30.9%), North America (n=34/139, 24.5%), Oceania (n=8/139, 5.8%), South America (n=7/139, 5.0%) and Africa (n=3/139, 2.2%). Supplementary tables provide distributions by experience and location. The systemic-risk classification designated patients with NIU taking immunosuppressive drugs other than biologics as increased risk. High risk meant NIU plus one factor: biologic use, a high immunosuppressive-drug dose, multiple immunosuppressive drugs, active associated systemic inflammatory disease, another comorbidity or multisystem disease affecting the heart, lungs and/or kidneys, neutropenia, smoking, pregnancy, age more than 60 years, or a prior infection during IMT. Very high risk meant NIU plus two or more factors. Adapted from the British Society of Rheumatology, this classification also served as an indirect indicator of uveitis severity.

document_sections.heading: Consensus on increased risk patients with NIU
document_sections.content: Table 1, figure 1 and supplementary tables present the increased-risk responses by infection or contact status and treatment decision. Experts agreed that an otherwise healthy patient with newly diagnosed NIU could start oral corticosteroids when needed. For otherwise healthy patients with inactive NIU, low-dose oral corticosteroids should continue regardless of COVID-19 contact; higher-dose oral corticosteroids should not be tapered or stopped unless NIU itself warrants it. If NIU is active, local corticosteroids are preferred to raising systemic corticosteroid doses irrespective of contact. For a patient with contact who is not taking oral corticosteroids, local treatment is preferred to starting systemic treatment. Otherwise healthy patients with active NIU should start or continue conventional immunosuppressive drugs. Known COVID-19 contact alone was not considered a reason to stop those drugs. The conventional agents considered were antimetabolites (methotrexate, azathioprine, mycophenolate mofetil), alkylating agents (cyclophosphamide) and T-cell inhibitors (cyclosporine, tacrolimus). Biologics considered were tumour necrosis factor (TNF)-alpha inhibitors (adalimumab, infliximab, golimumab, certolizumab), lymphocyte inhibitors (daclizumab, rituximab, abatacept) and specific receptor antagonists (anakinra, tocilizumab). For increased-risk patients with suspected or confirmed COVID-19, consensus opposed starting oral corticosteroids or intravenous methylprednisolone. Higher-dose oral corticosteroids should be reduced to a lower, safer dose. Experts did not agree on whether existing low-dose oral corticosteroids should continue, decrease or stop. They preferred local corticosteroids to initiating or intensifying systemic treatment. Conventional immunosuppressive drugs should neither be started nor maintained in these patients; existing treatment should instead be reduced or stopped.

document_sections.heading: Consensus on high-risk and very high-risk patients with NIU
document_sections.content: Tables 2 and 3, figures 2 and 3 and supplementary tables set out responses for high-risk and very high-risk patients by infection or contact status. In otherwise healthy high-risk patients, low-dose corticosteroids should continue without dose reduction or cessation, and higher-dose oral corticosteroids should not be tapered and stopped. Local corticosteroids are preferred to increasing systemic treatment regardless of contact; following contact, they are preferred to starting systemic therapy in someone not taking oral corticosteroids. Intravenous methylprednisolone should be avoided after contact. Otherwise healthy patients should continue conventional immunosuppressive drugs and biologics without dose reduction; biologics should not be initiated after contact. In otherwise healthy very high-risk patients, low-dose corticosteroids should continue without tapering to cessation. Local corticosteroids are preferred to starting systemic therapy or increasing its dose, regardless of contact. Intravenous methylprednisolone should be avoided after contact. Existing conventional immunosuppressive drugs and biologics should be maintained rather than stopped in otherwise healthy patients, but neither should be initiated after contact. For high-risk and very high-risk patients with suspected or confirmed COVID-19, consensus opposed starting oral corticosteroids. Existing systemic corticosteroid doses should be reduced and/or treatment stopped, with local corticosteroids preferred to starting or intensifying systemic therapy. Conventional immunosuppressive drugs and biologics should not be started or maintained; existing treatment should be reduced and/or stopped.

document_sections.heading: Consensus on general recommendations
document_sections.content: For scleritis, consensus favored initiating or continuing NSAIDs, rather than reducing or stopping them, only in otherwise healthy patients without known COVID-19 contact. No consensus supported any of those NSAID decisions for otherwise healthy patients with contact or for patients with possible or confirmed COVID-19. Experts agreed that patients already taking hydroxychloroquine should continue it, but reached no consensus on starting it in otherwise healthy patients, those with contact, or those with suspected or confirmed COVID-19. For patients with NIU receiving conventional IMT or biologics, experts supported hand hygiene, avoiding crowds, wearing masks, avoiding unnecessary hospital attendance, postponing long-term follow-up and self-isolating. They also supported urgent medical review for patients who were very unwell despite having no respiratory-infection symptoms.

document_sections.heading: Consensus based on experience of uveitis specialist and geographical location of practice
document_sections.content: Across experience levels and regions, experts agreed that corticosteroids, intravenous methylprednisolone, conventional immunosuppressive drugs and biologics should not be initiated for patients with suspected or confirmed COVID-19 in the increased-risk, high-risk and very high-risk groups. Most hygiene and physical-distancing recommendations were supported consistently irrespective of experience or location. For patients with COVID-19 and scleritis, experts in Asia, Africa, Europe and South America agreed on stopping NSAIDs (79% to 100%); those in North America and Oceania were less likely to advise stopping them (57% to 62%). Across experience levels and regions, experts agreed on continuing hydroxychloroquine for people already taking it.

document_sections.heading: DISCUSSION
document_sections.content: The authors describe their study as an international, expert-led effort to provide experience-based guidance during a shortage of evidence. They note a separate COVID-19 rheumatology initiative involving over 300 rheumatologists, scientists and patients. In their survey, decisions depended on possible COVID-19 infection, systemic risk, uveitis severity and the number of IMT agents needed. Although questions distinguished suspected from confirmed COVID-19, responses were similar; the authors suggest limited access to diagnostic testing, including in industrialised countries, as a possible reason. Corticosteroids are described as first-line therapy for achieving NIU quiescence, with systemic immunosuppression commonly used second-line when corticosteroids do not adequately control disease. Surveyed experts advised against beginning systemic corticosteroids or immunosuppression for NIU in patients with suspected or confirmed COVID-19, regardless of risk category. They favored tapering high-dose corticosteroids in these patients across risk groups and tapering even low-dose corticosteroids in high-risk or very high-risk patients. Tapering rather than abruptly stopping oral corticosteroids was advised because of adrenal-insufficiency risk. For otherwise healthy patients, consensus supported starting oral corticosteroids only in the increased-risk group, not in the high-risk or very high-risk groups. Low-dose oral corticosteroids and conventional IMT should be maintained. In increased-risk or high-risk patients, higher-dose corticosteroids should not be tapered to cessation; biologics, including tocilizumab, should continue where consensus supported continuation. Contact with COVID-19 lowered overall agreement. Following contact, experts opposed starting biologics in high-risk and very high-risk patients, while supporting continuation of low-dose oral corticosteroids and conventional IMT in increased-risk patients. During the pandemic, local treatment, including regional corticosteroid injections, was generally favored over systemic corticosteroids, except for otherwise healthy patients who were not already taking corticosteroids. Systemic corticosteroids might impede immune responses and pathogen clearance. Local delivery can concentrate medication at inflammation sites while limiting systemic exposure and may temporarily control vision-threatening uveitis complications while second-line immunosuppression is deferred. For patients ill with suspected or confirmed COVID-19, experts agreed against starting conventional IMT or biologics and favored at least dose reduction or cessation. The authors relate this caution to infection susceptibility during immunosuppression, particularly with TNF-α inhibitors. Consensus supported initiating or maintaining NSAIDs for scleritis in otherwise healthy people. The US Food and Drug Administration had stated that evidence did not link NSAID use to severe COVID-19. Because knowledge of SARS-CoV-2 and COVID-19 was changing rapidly, the authors caution that consensus opinions may change and require regular reassessment. They advocate physical distancing, hand hygiene and masks at follow-up, plus electronic or telehealth contact where possible to check for infection and reduce non-urgent clinic visits. Many COVID-19 treatments were under investigation. Clinical trials had yet to establish the place of interleukin (IL)-6 inhibitors; consensus concerning tocilizumab was limited to continuing it in otherwise healthy NIU patients. The authors state that tocilizumab improves visual acuity and reduces intraocular inflammation in NIU, but its use for NIU during COVID-19 remained uncertain. Evidence for hydroxychloroquine against COVID-19 was controversial and required randomized controlled trials; specialists reached consensus only on maintaining existing use. IMT increases concern about viral infections through effects on immune responses. The authors distinguish demonstrated severe influenza complications with IMT from coronavirus-related disease, for which the same increase had not been shown. They report that studies of earlier SARS-CoV and Middle East respiratory syndrome coronavirus outbreaks and more recent COVID-19 studies had not associated immunosuppression with increased death or intensive-care admission. In a cited case series, Monti et al examined eight Italian patients with rheumatoid arthritis or spondyloarthritis receiving IMT, four with confirmed and four with suspected COVID-19. They stopped immunosuppressive drugs when symptoms began; the cited authors reported no increased risk of life-threatening complications compared with the general population. A Global Rheumatology Alliance registry was being established to assess COVID-19 outcomes during IMT for rheumatic disease; inclusion of NIU patients could add relevant evidence. The authors discuss a possible role for dysregulated innate immunity and cytokine storm in tissue damage and disease progression, including potential concern for people immunosuppressed by treatment. They report higher plasma concentrations of IL-6, TNF-alfa, IL-2, IL-7, IL-10, granulocyte-colony stimulating factor, interferon-γ-inducible protein, monocyte chemoattractant protein and macrophage inflammatory protein 1 alpha in COVID-19, linked to severity. They describe inflammatory cytokine production by rapidly activated pathogenic Tcells and monocytes as impairing alveolar–capillary exchange and oxygen diffusion, potentially leading to pulmonary failure; an imbalance between Th1 and Th2 lymphocytes could also adversely affect B lymphocytes and antibody production. Potential COVID-19 roles for anti-rheumatic drugs had been hypothesized through antiviral or host-immune effects. The authors state that hydroxychloroquine may affect lysosomal proteases involved in viral cell entry and report evidence suggesting improvement in infection, while elsewhere emphasizing that its clinical utility remained controversial. They describe baricitinib as having antiviral and anti-inflammatory properties and suggest that anti-CD200 and anti-PD1 might have a role. High IL-6 had been reported as predictive of severe pneumonia, making its pathway a possible treatment target; the authors cite limited clinical trials reporting effectiveness of tocilizumab, an antibody that blocks signaling through the IL-6 receptor, in severe COVID-19. The study’s principal limitation was the lack of evidence-based literature on immunosuppression during the pandemic. Its expert opinions came from specialists on six continents, but some countries had not yet experienced major outbreaks, so responses might change as local cases rose. NIU includes diseases with differing courses, visual outcomes and treatment requirements. Rapid IMT reduction in conditions such as Behçet or Vogt–Koyanagi–Harada disease may cause potentially permanent visual loss. The guidance therefore might not apply equally across NIU diseases; specialists need to assess individual circumstances.

document_sections.heading: CONCLUSION
document_sections.content: The authors present this as the first worldwide survey of uveitis experts offering evolving consensus guidance on IMT for NIU during COVID-19. Decisions depended chiefly on possible infection and baseline systemic risk of COVID-19 complications, balanced against NIU severity and the IMT needed to prevent vision-threatening inflammatory flares. Given the difficulties of managing IMT during the pandemic, they favor decisions informed by multidisciplinary experts caring for patients with suspected or confirmed COVID-19.
